description:
FIXED s470br (Opus, 2026-09-05) -- filed and closed in the same session because
it was the cause of a merge-blocking regression, not a finding to carry.

PERL DOES NOT RE-ENTER A $SIG{__WARN__} HANDLER for a warning raised inside it.
Probed 5.40.3:

    my $n = 0;
    $SIG{__WARN__} = sub { $n++; warn "nested: $_[0]" };
    warn "outer\n";
    print "handler calls: $n\n";

  perl:  "nested: outer" ON STDERR, then "handler calls: 1"

So the handler runs ONCE and the nested `warn` takes the DEFAULT action.  PCL
re-entered it, which makes the commonest handler idiom in perl's own suite an
INFINITE LOOP:

    $SIG{__WARN__} = sub { ... } elsif ... else { warn $_[0] };   # substr.t:13

It blew the binding stack and HUNG perl-tests/substr.t (351 passing rows -> 0,
status TIMEOUT).  The bug is old; #1115 is what made it reachable, by giving PCL
its first warning that a handler can provoke (`Wide character in print`).

FIX: `*p-in-warn-handler*` in cl/pcl-runtime.lisp -- `p-warn` looks the handler
up only when the flag is clear and binds it around the call, so a nested warn
falls through to the default arm.  Guard rows in Pl/t/io-layers-01.t assert BOTH
halves (called once AND the nested text reaches stderr); both fail on a
`git archive 027ba9c` extraction.

NOT DONE, and worth its own look: perl has the SAME rule for $SIG{__DIE__}, and
PCL's die path was not audited here.
subject: perl does NOT re-enter a $SIG{__WARN__} handler for a warning raised inside it; PCL did, so the `else { warn $_[0] }` idiom looped and hung perl-tests/substr.t (351 rows -> 0, TIMEOUT)
